cards.vorderseite: SAH headache and the sentinel bleed
cards.rueckseite:
- **Thunderclap headache:** maximal within seconds to 1 min, "worst headache of my life"; ≈ 97% of aneurysmal SAH have headache
- **Sentinel (warning) headache:** minor leak in 30–50% days to weeks before the major rupture; often misdiagnosed
- Associated: vomiting, syncope (≈ 45%), meningismus (after 6–24 h), photophobia, seizures, **Terson syndrome** (vitreous/preretinal hemorrhage, ≈ 20–40%, worse prognosis)
- Work-up: CT; if negative and > 6 h: LP for **xanthochromia** (needs ≈ 6–12 h to develop), CTA

- ICU, neuro checks hourly; **EVD** for acute hydrocephalus (avoid overdrainage before securing)
- **Blood pressure:** SBP **< 160** (many aim < 140) until the aneurysm is secured; avoid hypotension
- **Nimodipine 60 mg PO q 4 h for 21 days** (improves outcome, not angiographic spasm; reduce to 30 mg q 2 h if hypotensive)
- Euvolemia, normonatremia (avoid fluid restriction), normoglycemia, normothermia
- Reverse anticoagulants/antiplatelets; consider short antifibrinolytic course
- Secure the aneurysm early (< 24–72 h)
- Seizure prophylaxis only briefly if used (avoid phenytoin)

cards.text: Rebleeding of an untreated ruptured aneurysm: highest on day 1 ({{c1::4–13.6%}}, one third within 3 h), then about {{c2::1.5% per day}} for 13 days; {{c3::15–20%}} rebleed within 2 weeks and 50% within 6 months, then ≈ 3%/year. Antifibrinolytics: {{c4::tranexamic acid 1 g IV, then 1 g q 6 h}} for ≤ 72 h only if treatment is unavoidably delayed (ULTRA trial: no outcome benefit).

cards.rueckseite:
Occurs in 10–30%, usually days 3–10, often **cerebral salt wasting** (natriuresis + volume loss), sometimes SIADH.
**Danger:** hyponatremia + hypovolemia increases **delayed cerebral ischemia**.
**Management:** **do not fluid restrict**; isotonic/hypertonic saline (NaCl tablets, 3%), **fludrocortisone** (0.1–0.2 mg) or hydrocortisone to reduce natriuresis; correct slowly.

cards.vorderseite: Neurogenic stress cardiomyopathy and neurogenic pulmonary edema
cards.rueckseite:
**Stress cardiomyopathy (Takotsubo-like):** catecholamine surge → troponin rise, ECG changes (ST/T, QT prolongation), **regional wall motion abnormality not matching a coronary territory** (often apical ballooning or basal), reduced EF; more with poor-grade SAH; usually reversible in days–weeks. Treat with supportive care, inotropes (dobutamine/milrinone) if needed.
**Neurogenic pulmonary edema:** within hours after severe SAH/TBI/seizures; sympathetic surge → pulmonary venoconstriction and capillary leak; treat with ventilation, PEEP, careful fluids.

- **Prevention:** nimodipine, **euvolemia** (prophylactic hypervolemia/"triple-H" abandoned: no benefit, more complications)
- **Symptomatic DCI:** exclude other causes (hydrocephalus, rebleed, hyponatremia, seizures), then **induced hypertension** (e.g., norepinephrine, raise MAP stepwise) once the aneurysm is secured
- **Refractory:** **endovascular:** balloon **angioplasty** (proximal vessels) and/or **intra-arterial vasodilators** (verapamil, nimodipine, milrinone) for distal spasm
- Statins and magnesium: no benefit in RCTs; clazosentan reduces angiographic spasm but not outcome

**Acute** (≈ 20%): obstruction by intraventricular blood; risk with IVH, poor grade, posterior circulation → **EVD** (small rebleed risk from sudden ICP drop; keep drain at ≈ 15–20 cm H₂O before securing).
**Chronic shunt-dependent** (≈ 10–20%): impaired absorption; risk with IVH, poor grade, age, acute hydrocephalus. Weaning: raise/clamp EVD gradually; failed wean → **VP shunt**.
Lumbar drains only if no obstructive component. Lamina terminalis fenestration does not reduce shunt dependency.

cards.text: Saccular aneurysm locations: 85–95% anterior circulation: {{c1::ACom (≈ 30%, most common)}}, {{c2::PComm (≈ 25%)}}, MCA (≈ 20%); 5–15% posterior circulation, most often the {{c3::basilar tip}}, and on the vertebral artery the {{c4::VA–PICA junction}}. {{c5::20–30%}} of patients have multiple aneurysms.

cards.rueckseite:
- **Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease** (≈ 10–15%; screen those with a family history of aneurysm/SAH)
- **Fibromuscular dysplasia**, **Ehlers–Danlos type IV**, Marfan (debated), pseudoxanthoma elasticum
- **Coarctation of the aorta**, bicuspid aortic valve
- **AVMs** (flow-related), moyamoya
- Hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia, NF1
- Familial intracranial aneurysm syndrome
- Infective endocarditis (mycotic), cocaine

**Early treatment (within 72 h, ideally < 24 h)** is standard: prevents rebleeding (highest early) and allows aggressive treatment of vasospasm.
Historical "late surgery" (after day 10–14) avoided the swollen brain but lost many patients to rebleeding during the waiting period.
Even poor-grade patients who improve with EVD benefit from early treatment.

Most often during dissection or clip application (≈ 5–20%).
**Management:**
- Two suckers; control with **temporary clips on the parent vessel(s)** (proximal control established beforehand)
- Ask for **burst suppression** (propofol) and brief induced hypotension only until control; then restore BP during temporary occlusion
- Tamponade with cottonoid; avoid blind clipping
- Adenosine-induced cardiac standstill as an option
- Keep temporary occlusion short (< 10–20 min; intermittent reperfusion)
During coiling: reverse heparin (protamine), keep coiling to seal, EVD.

zeilen: Highest; IIIa within coil interstices may still thrombose, IIIb along the wall tends to grow
cards.notiz: Greenberg p. 1467–1468. Recurrence after coiling ≈ 20% (retreatment ≈ 10%), much higher than after clipping (< 1–2%) → angiographic follow-up.

cards.rueckseite:
Most common (≈ 30%), more in men; usually fed by a **dominant A1** (aneurysm points away from it).
**Presentation:** SAH with frontal ICH, IVH; rarely visual loss from chiasm compression; post-op **abulia, amnesia, confabulation** (perforators, hypothalamus/basal forebrain), hyponatremia, DI.
**Clipping:** usually from the side of the **dominant A1** (proximal control) or the side to which the dome does not point; gyrus rectus resection may be needed; preserve the **recurrent artery of Heubner** and hypothalamic perforators.

≈ 25%; arises from the ICA at the PComm origin, typically pointing **posterolateral and inferior**.
**Classic:** **pupil-involving oculomotor palsy** (also without SAH = expanding, urgent).
**Surgical pearls:** check for a **fetal PCA** (PComm cannot be sacrificed), identify and preserve the **anterior choroidal artery** just distal; avoid retracting the temporal lobe early (dome may adhere to the tentorium/temporal lobe → premature rupture).

≈ 20%; usually at the **M1 bifurcation/trifurcation**, often wide-necked with branches arising from the base → **clipping often preferred** over coiling.
Rupture frequently causes a **temporal or sylvian ICH** (indication for clipping + hematoma evacuation, decompression) and seizures.
Approach: pterional, transsylvian (distal-to-proximal or proximal-to-distal) or superior temporal gyrus route.

cards.vorderseite: Ophthalmic segment and cavernous carotid aneurysms
cards.rueckseite:
**Ophthalmic segment (paraclinoid):** arise near the ophthalmic or superior hypophyseal artery; women; often large; visual loss from compression of the optic nerve from below (**ipsilateral inferior nasal field** defect first). Surgery needs **anterior clinoidectomy**, opening of the optic canal and **cervical ICA proximal control**; flow diverters are common now.
**Cavernous carotid:** **extradural** → rupture usually causes a **CCF**, not SAH (low SAH risk); present with painful **ophthalmoplegia** (VI first) or retro-orbital pain; asymptomatic ones are observed; treat if symptomatic/large (flow diverter, parent vessel occlusion after balloon test occlusion).

**Basilar bifurcation:** most common posterior circulation aneurysm; surgery is high-risk (thalamoperforators from P1) → **endovascular treatment preferred** (BRAT, ISAT); surgical routes: pterional/orbitozygomatic (tip above the dorsum) or subtemporal (low tip). Oculomotor palsy and hydrocephalus common.
**PICA (VA–PICA junction):** most common VA aneurysm; can present with IVH in the fourth ventricle; **far-lateral approach**; endovascular if PICA origin can be preserved; lower cranial nerve deficits after surgery; distal PICA aneurysms are often flow-related or dissecting.

cards.titel: PHASES score (5-year rupture risk of unruptured aneurysms)
cards.notiz: Greenberg Tables 89.2–89.3, p. 1486–1488. Score ≤ 2 → ≈ 0.4% 5-year risk; ≥ 12 → ≈ 17.8%. UIATS adds treatment-related factors.

cards.rueckseite:
Screen (MRA/CTA) when **≥ 2 first-degree relatives** have aneurysms or SAH (yield ≈ 10%); also patients with **ADPKD** and a family history.
Familial aneurysms rupture at a smaller size and younger age, more often MCA, and are often multiple.
Repeat screening every **5–7 years** (new aneurysms develop).
A single affected relative: screening not generally recommended.

Diameter **≥ 25 mm**; ≈ 5% of aneurysms; women in their 50s–60s; ICA (cavernous, paraclinoid), MCA, basilar.
**Presentation:** **mass effect** (cranial nerve deficits, visual loss, brainstem compression, seizures), **thromboembolism**, SAH (high rupture risk if intradural: ≈ 40% at 5 years per ISUIA).
Often partially thrombosed (onion-skin layers on MRI; angiography underestimates size).
**Treatment:** clip reconstruction with thrombectomy, **bypass + parent artery occlusion/trapping**, **flow diverters**, Hunterian ligation after balloon test occlusion.

Blood in one or a few **cortical sulci** without basal cistern involvement; aneurysm rarely the cause.
- **Age < 60:** **RCVS** (thunderclap headaches, often postpartum or drug triggered; "string of beads" angiography that resolves within 12 weeks; treat with calcium channel blockers, stop triggers, avoid steroids)
- **Age > 60:** **cerebral amyloid angiopathy** (transient focal neurologic episodes, superficial siderosis, microbleeds)
- Others: cortical venous thrombosis, PRES, vasculitis, dural AVF, endocarditis, trauma

≈ 15% of spontaneous SAH has a negative initial angiogram.
- **Diffuse/aneurysmal pattern:** repeat **DSA in 7–14 days** (and MRI of brain/spine: spinal AVM, tumor, dissection); yield of repeat study up to 10–20%
- **Perimesencephalic (pretruncal) pattern:** see separate card; excellent prognosis
- Rebleeding risk of SAH of unknown cause ≈ 1%/yr or less; prognosis better than aneurysmal SAH, but vasospasm and hydrocephalus can still occur

Blood centered **anterior to the midbrain/pons** (interpeduncular, prepontine cisterns), limited spread into ambient/basal sylvian cisterns, no frank IVH or extension to the lateral sylvian or interhemispheric fissures; CT within **≤ 2 days**.
Likely **venous** origin (below the Liliequist membrane). ≈ 10% of SAH; patients are usually in good grade.
A high-quality negative CTA/DSA is required (≈ 5% of this pattern is due to a **basilar or vertebral aneurysm**); repeat angiography is debated.
**Prognosis excellent**: rebleeding and vasospasm very rare, normal life expectancy.

Hemorrhage risk is highest in the **third trimester**; maternal mortality high.
- Neurosurgical considerations take priority: **treat the aneurysm as in nonpregnant patients** (clipping or coiling with fetal shielding)
- Avoid mannitol in large doses, nitroprusside; nimodipine acceptable; monitor the fetus
- Delivery: after the aneurysm is secured, **mode by obstetric indications** (vaginal delivery acceptable); if untreated near term: C-section, possibly combined with aneurysm surgery
- Differential: eclampsia, CVT, PRES, RCVS

< 1% of aneurysms; mostly **pseudoaneurysms** (no true wall), from penetrating injury (GSW, stab) or closed head injury with skull base fracture.
Typical sites: **distal ACA** against the falx edge, cortical branches under a fracture, **petrous/cavernous ICA** (skull base fracture → epistaxis, CCF).
Presentation often **delayed** (days–weeks) with hemorrhage; high mortality (≈ 50%) if ruptured.
Treatment: early surgery (trapping/excision, wrapping) or endovascular occlusion; CTA after penetrating injuries near major vessels.
